summary: Iron lighthouse at the mouth of Pass a l'Outre in the Mississippi delta, moved there from Head of Passes and lit in 1855; out of service by 1930-34.

lens.where: removed 1930 by the tender Magnolia (Lighthouse Friends); USLHS lists current optic as removed

structures.type: conical cast iron with brick lining
structures.note: Built at Head of Passes in 1852, moved and lit here in 1855. Height 63 ft (19 m) to lantern center (USLHS); Rowlett gives original 85 ft, now about 40 ft. Lantern fell by 2007 after Katrina loosened it.

access.note: Owned by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and managed by the Delta National Wildlife Refuge; reached only by boat; tower closed (Rowlett, Lighthouse Friends); not open to the public (USLHS).

events.note: Iron tower built at Head of Passes; Rowlett calls it the nation's tallest cast-iron lighthouse of its time
Congress appropriated $6,000 on 3 March 1853 to move the tower to Pass a l'Outre and build a small beacon at Head of Passes (Lighthouse Friends)
Tower moved to Pass a l'Outre
Lit in December 1855; John Lory first keeper
Third-order Fresnel lens (USLHS)
June 1861: Confederate forces removed the lamps and destroyed the oil on hand; Union forces later took down the Fresnel lens (Lighthouse Friends)
Confederate soldiers burned the keeper's dwelling on 1 January 1862
Returned to service 20 April 1863 after a new dwelling was built and the tower relined
Steam whistle at Pass a l'Outre; Congress provided $10,000 on 3 March 1871 for this and Southwest Pass
Tower floor raised five feet after tides flooded it
Fog signal discontinued (Lighthouse Friends)
Hurricane on 28 September 1917 blew away the tool house and damaged the dwelling, walks and wharf (Lighthouse Friends); Bulletin index lists damage by hurricane
Storm damage to the station, per the Bulletin index (pp. 186, 225, 297 of the Bulletin volume)
Tower given a spiral black and white daymark (Lighthouse Friends); USLHS records a black daymark from its 1908 data
Dwelling raised onto concrete piers, boathouse and sidewalk rebuilt, dwellings repaired, new door cut in tower; work paid from a 1918 appropriation
Keepers did not report a schooner (O.C.L.) anchored nearby; seized 1 November 1929 with no liquor found; the district superintendent judged the keepers negligent (Lighthouse Friends)
Tender Magnolia removed the Fresnel lens; decommissioned 11 January 1930 (Lighthouse Friends)
Rowlett: inactive since 1930
Coast Guard used the abandoned tower as a rumrunner lookout until the end of Prohibition (Lighthouse Friends)
USLHS: year discontinued 1934 (differs from the 1930 decommissioning above)
Lantern, loosened by Hurricane Katrina, fell into the water; only the stump stood by 2007 (Rowlett; Lighthouse Friends says around 2007)

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1852 date is the iron tower's build at Head of Passes (Rowlett). Its lighting at Pass a l'Outre is 1855 (Lighthouse Friends; USLHS), so the 'first against last' tower question is answered: the record's 1852 is the tower's first build, not a second light here.

notes_for_editor: Rich official record. Checked 2026-10-28. (1) Out of service: Lighthouse Friends and Rowlett give 1930 (decommissioned 11 January 1930, lens removed by the tender Magnolia); USLHS gives 1934 as the year of discontinuance; the story gives both. (2) Daymark: Lighthouse Friends says a spiral black and white daymark in 1919; USLHS gives black from a source dated 1908 (LL-1908); both in the story. (3) Heights and focal plane: Rowlett gives 85 ft original and about 40 ft now; USLHS gives 63 ft to lantern centre and 70 ft above mean high water (21.3 m, used as focal_height_m). Lighthouse Friends gives the focal plane as seventy-seven feet (about 23.5 m); the record does not carry that figure, so it is unresolved. (4) McNamara: the 1926 Bulletin (PDF p. 18) gives deckhand and fireman service from 1 July 1876 to 1 September 1893 and from 1 August 1896 to 1910; Lighthouse Friends says keeper 1911 to 1926; the roster has him head keeper from 1918 only. Not resolved. (5) Putnam's Frank's Island tower is 'rebuilt in 1822' (scan p. 159); Lighthouse Friends gives March 1823 for its first light. The story uses the Lighthouse Friends date only. (6) Spellings: Lighthouse Friends has 'Conference forces', 'Salsbury', 'Emma Salsbury' and 'Mrs. H.E. Marshall'; the roster has 'Saulsbury' and 'Henrietta E. Marshall'; the story uses the roster spelling. (7) Commissioner of Lighthouses FY1920 (scan p. 547, printed p. 49) was read on the page's OCR head. FY1921 (scan p. 656) is labelled by the corpus; its printed page is unconfirmed ('51?') and the page image was NOT viewed, so a human should open scan p. 656 before publication. (8) Putnam's Frank's Island passage is on scan p. 159 (printed page unconfirmed). The Semmes passage is on scan p. 160 (printed p. 115 unconfirmed) and is general context: it does not name Pass a l'Outre. (9) The 1917 storm: the Bulletin's November 1917 storm report (PDF pp. 48-49, printed p. 297) gives 28 September 1917 for the Gulf coast landfall and the station damage; the OCR of the station sentence is garbled, so evidence uses clean fragments. The index's 'commended 297' and the Secretary of Commerce commendation rest on the index and Lighthouse Friends. (10) USLHS roster: 115 lines matched by name and years; the story names only a few. The roster is not used for counts in the text. (11) The USCG Historian's archived page could not be read (403, then a calendar page); the NPS Louisiana inventory returned 404. (12) Chronicling America searches for 'Pass a Loutre' gave many OCR hits in Louisiana papers 1855-1934 and none for 1917 or 1929-31; no newspaper page bearing on this station was read. (13) Wikipedia (en, fr) was read for leads only and is not cited. (14) Lighthouse Friends is copyrighted: the story paraphrases it, with one short quotation ('otter pass').
